from datetime import datetime

from ldstats import LogitNormal, LogNormal
from resgo.model import (

    FieldDevelopmentModel,
    FlatPriceModel,
    FlatRoyaltyModel,

)
from resgo.plotting import ProspectReporter

from src.plotting import theme

PLOTTING_BACKEND = "altair"

CHAINS=8

alt.data_transformers.disable_max_rows()
theme.apply_lex_altair_theme()

Resgo still has no UI, but before I start developing it I have one more feature to
build: 

Portfolio simulation.

Portfolio simulation is the Resgo end-game. Resgo already provides a very performant
Prospect level simulation engine, from subsurface through to commercial metrics, and
that leaves it well positioned for zooming out one more level to portfolio level
analysis.

My goals at the outset are the following:

1. Allow grouping Prospects into Portfolios, with lossless representation
2. Represent parent-child relationships between Prospects to allow for dependency
   propagation
3. Dependency propagation should allows information to flow between prospects and their
   children, so that drilling outcomes follow logical chains during simulation
4. Use those logical chains to derive stand-alone and full-cycle metrics for decision
   gating
5. Report accepted, strategic (full cycle economics says drill) and rejected prospect
   decisions at the portfolio level

## Structure and constraints

The most convenient representation of a Portfolio with these constraints in mind is a
tree. Prospects can have children: opportunities who's risks are affected by outcomes in
their parent. That creates some limitations (sibling Prospects can't have dependencies)
but I think the simplicity of tree depth traversal, and limiting onerous dependency
configuration, will make that trade-off worthwhile.

For lossless Prospect representation in Resgo, this means that dependency must be
represented at the reservoir and risk factor level. This is a complication that I
believe will pay dividends in granular configuration and interpretability of portfolio
simulations, matching the mental models in subsurface teams' heads when defining
dependencies between opportunitities.

It will mean, for example, that reservoirs in the Propects tree can share strong
P(charge) dependency. If the parent fails on charge, that heavily impacts the P(charge)
of children. This is well suited for modelling play-openers on untested migration
pathways, for example. Similarly these dependencies can be captured for reservoir
presence for testing sand fairways, and seal/trap for things like demonstrating fault
seal.

## Dependency mechanics

I'm going to bring up Bayes again, sorry[^not-sorry]. 

Dependency in this framing is a Bayesian probability update from the prior risk
probability (say a 0.5 probability of charge in the child reservoir). Mechanically, the
update is applied in odds space:

$$
O_{\mathrm{post}} = O_{\mathrm{prior}} \times \text{LH}
$$

or, equivalently, in log-odds space:

$$
\ln_2\left(O_{\mathrm{post}}\right)
= \ln_2\left(O_{\mathrm{prior}}\right) + \ln_2\left(\text{LH}\right)
$$

where $O = p / (1 - p)$ is the odds, $\text{LH}$ is the likelihood ratio, and
$\ln_2$ denotes a base-2 logarithm. 

Using a base-2 logarithm means that the evidence term, $\ln_2(\text{LH})$, is measured
in **bits**: positive bits increase the odds of success, negative bits decrease them,
and zero bits leave the prior odds unchanged.

You'll have to humor me because it seems weird, but this is a very mentally ergonomic
way of framing Bayesian probability updates. 

Starting from a prior probability of 0.50 as an example, each additional bit doubles the
likelihood ratio:

| Evidence | Likelihood ratio | Posterior probability |
|---:|---:|---:|
| -4 bits | 1:16 | 0.06 |
| -3 bits | 1:8 | 0.11 |
| -2 bits | 1:4 | 0.20 |
| -1 bit | 1:2 | 0.33 |
| 0 bits | 1:1 | 0.50 |
| 1 bit | 2:1 | 0.67 |
| 2 bits | 4:1 | 0.80 |
| 3 bits | 8:1 | 0.89 |
| 4 bits | 16:1 | 0.94 |

Operating in this way means that updates are commutative: you can add and subtract bits
of evidence to arrive at a final posterior. This is mental Bayes trickery, but is also
useful for efficient and interpretable communication of risk dependencies in the context
of the portfolio simulator.

> _"If the Bonanza prospect fails on charge, how bad would that be for charge risk at
> Buffet?"_
>
> _"They're on the same migration corridor so really bad... probably -4 bits."_
>
> _"We did see shows on that separate migration corridor connecting to Buffet though,
> remember?"_
>
> _"Fair enough, that's probably worth 1 bit. -3 bits total then."_

Now, regardless of P(charge) at Bonanza, the information it provides to Buffet is
explicitly communicated. 

If, for example, P(charge) is 0.5 across prospects and Bonanza fails on charge, that
means Buffet gets a P(charge) of 0.11 (killing it). If Bonanza _is_ charged though, that
increase P(charge) at Buffet to 0.89!

See? We can all become Bayesians with some language tricks.

There is a technical wrinkle that positive and negative updates are not necessarily
symmetric (relevant example
[here](https://nick-dorsch.github.io/blog/posts/confusion/)), so the code should make
that explicit, but default to symmetric updates.

## Decision Gates

For the portfolio simulation to be coherent, decisions need to be made about whether to
drill for each Prospect, based on the information available. That requires point
estimate hurdles. Decisions aren't made stochastically. We can't just use the simulation
result to determine the right path on every iteration, because the decision maker
doesn't know what will happen. That means a decision criterion needs to be specified. 

This can be things like a positive risked mean NPV (equivalent to EMV):

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{NPV}_{\mathrm{risked}}\right] > 0
$$

or a positive risked 90th percentile NPV:

$$
Q_{0.10}\left(\mathrm{NPV}_{\mathrm{risked}}\right) > 0
$$

But it needs to be agreed upon up front for the portfolio simulation to operate. Most
companies have defined hurdles like this in place, but there may be situations where
hurdles are prospect specific.

Luckily, because Resgo simulates everything in a single integrated chain, these decision
metrics will be consistently applied to rigorously defined stochastic ranges of NPV.
That is a rare luxury in portfolio analysis contexts.

## Simulation process

Resgo allows us to very ergonomically simulate the entire portfolio tree in a forward
pass, adjusting risk factors on success/failure case of parent nodes, then run the
decision gating logic on the results to determine which prospects get drilled and which
get rejected. We can then aggregate the portfolio level NPV to assess its overall
economic value and uncertainty.

## Additional wrinkles

Because we are simulating an ensemble of prospects, we need to be careful to define a
few things up front. 

We need a single price deck, especially if it is stochastic, to avoid individual
prospects getting their own price histories.

We also need a single economic basis for escalation and discounting. That means every
prospect has NPV calculations consistent on a single "start date" for the whole
portfolio. Failing to do this would unfairly inflate the value of future prospects in
the schedule.

## Strategic value

Something compelling that this gives us is the ability to quantify the strategic value
of prospects. This is the stand-alone value of the prospect, plus any downstream
opportunity it creates.

This means that a stand-alone prospect with negative NPV---maybe due to a low
P(Success)---can have its downstream value quantified and summed to make it _full-cycle_
economic, even if it is not drillable on its own merits.

For example:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    Buffet["Buffet<br/>P(success): 0.45<br/>NPV: $180MM"]

    Buffet --> Bitesize["Bitesize<br/>P(success): 0.35<br/>NPV: $70MM"]
    Buffet --> Budget["Budget<br/>P(success): 0.55<br/>NPV: $75MM"]
    Buffet --> Boring["Boring<br/>P(success): 0.10<br/>NPV: -$200MM"]

    Boring --> Bonanza["Bonanza<br/>P(success): 0.15<br/>NPV: $1,200MM"]

    Bonanza --> Banquet["Banquet<br/>P(success): 0.20<br/>NPV: $700MM"]
    Bonanza --> Bento["Bento<br/>P(success): 0.18<br/>NPV: $650MM"]
    Bonanza --> Baklava["Baklava<br/>P(success): 0.12<br/>NPV: $1,000MM"]
```

Hear me out.

Boring is a high risk, low return prospect. It will probably fail, and it's a small
closure. It's a dog.

But if Buffet is successful, you'd be crazy not to drill it.

This is the crazy senior geologist speaking. He has a mad twinkle in his eye, and he knows
nobody will listen, but he knows he is right, _dammit_.

Why is he right?

Because the information that Boring provides, expensive as it may be, has huge upside.

A success at Boring would boost the P(success) of Bonanza, a high risk, high reward
prospect that nobody is considering because "there is no migration that way". Bonanza is
a _play opener_, it has several follow-ups, all of which are currently high risk, but
high value.

So you drill Boring to open up the play.

I've been the crazy guy before. I've never been able to quantify any of this stuff
persuasively. Resgo lets me quantify the whole lot, all the way through to economics. It
becomes a simple matter of well applied decision theory, a consequence of your decision
metrics, and the risks and uncertainties in your portfolio. 

Resgo tells you to do it.

And the tool isn't crazy! It's just uncertainty propagation, Bayesian updating and
economics. Don't argue with the results, just make sure you verify your inputs.

Now let's try to do it.

# Example

Since I've started naming prospects with the B theme, let's use that in a live example.

Here's the Portfolio tree again, without risks and NPVs as we haven't calculated them
yet:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    Buffet[Buffet]

    Buffet --> Bitesize[Bitesize]
    Buffet --> Budget[Budget]
    Buffet --> Boring[Boring]

    Boring --> Bonanza[Bonanza]

    Bonanza --> Banquet[Banquet]
    Bonanza --> Bento[Bento]
    Bonanza --> Baklava[Baklava]
```

My goal with this example will be to live demo the sequence I spelled out in the
previous section on strategic value.

Let's define these prospects one by one. All prospects will share the same set of
reservoir targets, named "Archer", "Boulder", "Canyon" and "Drift".

```{python}
# Set up shared zone information

zone_corr_matrix = [
    [1.0, 0.20, -0.10],
    [0.20, 1.0, -0.30],
    [-0.10, -0.30, 1.0],
]

zones = {
    "Archer": Zone(
        name="Archer",
        net_m=LogNormal.elicit(8.0, 18.0),
        porosity=LogitNormal.elicit(0.16, 0.24),
        water_saturation=LogitNormal.elicit(0.28, 0.42),
        corr_matrix=zone_corr_matrix,
    ),
    "Boulder": Zone(
        name="Boulder",
        net_m=LogNormal.elicit(12.0, 28.0),
        porosity=LogitNormal.elicit(0.14, 0.22),
        water_saturation=LogitNormal.elicit(0.30, 0.46),
        corr_matrix=zone_corr_matrix,
    ),
    "Canyon": Zone(
        name="Canyon",
        net_m=LogNormal.elicit(6.0, 14.0),
        porosity=LogitNormal.elicit(0.18, 0.27),
        water_saturation=LogitNormal.elicit(0.24, 0.38),
        corr_matrix=zone_corr_matrix,
    ),
    "Drift": Zone(
        name="Drift",
        net_m=LogNormal.elicit(20.0, 45.0),
        porosity=LogitNormal.elicit(0.10, 0.18),
        water_saturation=LogitNormal.elicit(0.34, 0.52),
        corr_matrix=zone_corr_matrix,
    ),
}
```

```{python}
# Set up risk profiles

risk_profiles = {
    "Archer": RiskProfile.from_probs(
        p_reservoir=0.92,
        p_seal=0.95,
        p_closure=0.96,
        p_charge=0.40,
    ),
    "Boulder": RiskProfile.from_probs(
        p_reservoir=0.88,
        p_seal=0.93,
        p_closure=0.97,
        p_charge=0.40,
    ),
    "Canyon": RiskProfile.from_probs(
        p_reservoir=0.94,
        p_seal=0.90,
        p_closure=0.95,
        p_charge=0.40,
    ),
    "Drift": RiskProfile.from_probs(
        p_reservoir=0.86,
        p_seal=0.92,
        p_closure=0.94,
        p_charge=0.40,
    ),
}
```

## Prospects

### Buffet

Buffet is a risky but high value prospect that is the overall play opener for the
portfolio. The biggest concern the team has is with charge, as they are not convinced a
migration pathway exists at this location.

```{python}
#| output: false

buffet_area_km2 = (18.0, 25.0)

buffet_reservoirs = [
    Reservoir(
        area_km2=LogNormal.elicit(*buffet_area_km2),
        zone=zones["Archer"],
        oil=Oil.default(),
        oil_type_curve=OilTypeCurve.default(),
        risk_profile=risk_profiles["Archer"],
    ),
    Reservoir(
        area_km2=LogNormal.elicit(*buffet_area_km2),
        zone=zones["Boulder"],
        oil=Oil.default(),
        oil_type_curve=OilTypeCurve.default(),
        risk_profile=risk_profiles["Boulder"],
    ),
    Reservoir(
        area_km2=LogNormal.elicit(*buffet_area_km2),
        zone=zones["Canyon"],
        oil=Oil.default(),
        oil_type_curve=OilTypeCurve.default(),
        risk_profile=risk_profiles["Canyon"],
    ),
    Reservoir(
        area_km2=LogNormal.elicit(*buffet_area_km2),
        zone=zones["Drift"],
        oil=Oil.default(),
        oil_type_curve=OilTypeCurve.default(),
        risk_profile=risk_profiles["Drift"],
    ),
]

buffet = Prospect(
    name="Buffet",
    volumetric_model=VolumetricModel(
        reservoirs=buffet_reservoirs,
        dependency=0.5,
    ),
    field_development_model=FieldDevelopmentModel.simple_development(
        num_producers=10,
        reservoir_names=None,
        start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
        month_offset=12,
        drill_to_online_months=12,
        max_oil_rate_stbpd=35_000,
        producer_capex_USD=55e6,
        years=30,
    ),
    economic_model=EconomicModel.from_values(
        price_model=FlatPriceModel(oil_price_USD_stb=75.0, gas_price_USD_mmbtu=4.0),
        royalty_model=FlatRoyaltyModel(royalty_rate=0.10),
        tax_model=FlatTaxModel(tax_rate=0.30),
        infrastructure_capex_USD=150e6,
        annual_opex_USD=12e6,
        producer_abandonment_cost_USD=2e6,
        dry_hole_cost_USD=40e6,
    ),
)

buffet_simpack = buffet.simulate(
    risked=True,
    levered=False,
    chains=CHAINS,
    draws=DRAWS,
    seed=SEED,
)

buffet_reporter = ProspectReporter(prospect=buffet, simpack=buffet_simpack)
```

#### Volumetrics

```{python}
buffet_reporter.plotter.volumetric_ecdf(backend=PLOTTING_BACKEND)
```
##### Total

```{python}
buffet_reporter.tabler.volumetrics()
```

##### By Reservoir

```{python}
buffet_reporter.tabler.volumetrics(group_by="reservoir")
```

#### Economics

```{python}
buffet_reporter.plotter.cash_flow(figsize=(650, 250), backend=PLOTTING_BACKEND)
```

```{python}
buffet_reporter.tabler.risked_npv()
```

## High risk

You'll notice this whole portfolio looks very high risk. That is because all risk
factors are being applied with our current state of information. The entire portfolio
has high charge risk, a P(Charge) of 0.4 for Buffet, Bitesize, Budget and Boring, and an
even harsher 0.2 for Bonanza and its children, making them all a bad bet. This is an
untested migration pathway in our basin.

The opportunities don't necessarily hold up on their own merits. That is why strategic
value is so important.

## Portfolio model

The portfolio manages all these prospects, along with their parent-child relationships
and information sharing for risk factors. For simplicity we will just model information
sharing for P(charge), but a user could model relationships between reservoir risk
factors as they see fit.
